summary: RFC 9334 defines protocol-agnostic conceptual messages exchanged between RATS roles. This Standards Track document defines the Conceptual Message Wrapper, a way to carry and identify those messages in practice.

eli5.summary: A standard envelope for passing messages about whether a gadget is trustworthy, so everyone can tell what type is inside.

questions: what is a rats conceptual message wrapper
how to carry attestation evidence in a jwt
subtitle: A common envelope that labels and carries remote attestation messages in CBOR, JSON, JWT, CWT and X.509 formats.

tldr.problem: Remote attestation messages such as Evidence and Attestation Results travel over many protocols and in many serialization formats, and each protocol would otherwise have to redefine how to handle them.
tldr.mechanism: The Conceptual Message Wrapper (CMW) is a self-describing envelope with three forms (Record, Tag and Collection) in CBOR and JSON, plus a CBOR tag, JWT and CWT claims, an X.509 extension, media types and CoAP Content-Formats.
tldr.outcome: A protocol can carry any attestation message without knowing its inner format. The wrapper gives no security by itself, so protection must be added separately.

facts.label: Indicator bitmap
facts.value: At most 4 bytes; values 1 to 31 currently

today: RFC 9999 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026. The unit metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC, so it is the current definition of the CMW.

sections.title: Why a Wrapper Is Needed
sections.content:
The RATS architecture in RFC 9334 defines conceptual messages: Evidence, Attestation Results, Endorsements, Reference Values and Appraisal Policies. They describe what a data unit means, but not its wire format, encoding or transport.

In practice one message crosses several protocols. In the background-check topology, Evidence flows from the Attester to the Relying Party and then from the Relying Party to the Verifier, each leg over a different protocol. In the passport topology, an attestation result goes from the Verifier to the Attester and later, over another channel, to the Relying Party.

The CMW gives these messages a common structure. Protocol designers do not have to update their specifications for every new message type or serialization, and a Relying Party implementer does not have to parse attestation messages from TPM-based or confidential-computing devices. The design goals are self-description (precise typing without relying on the surrounding protocol), reuse of media types, and extensibility through plug-in handlers selected by type identifier.
sections.eli5: Imagine many different delivery trucks carrying sealed boxes. If every box has the same kind of label, each truck can carry any box without knowing what is inside.

sections.title: The Record CMW
sections.content:
A CMW is a tree. Leaves are Record or Tag CMWs, and inner nodes are Collection CMWs. A Record is an array with two or three members: type, value and an optional ind.

  • type is a media type string, or in CBOR an unsigned integer that is a CoAP Content-Format ID. The integer form is not used in JSON.
  • value is the conceptual message serialized as the type says. In JSON it MUST be Base64 with the URL and filename-safe alphabet, without padding, even if the message is already text. In CBOR it MUST be a byte string.
  • ind is an optional bitmap of at most 4 bytes saying which conceptual message types the value holds. It is useful only when the type alone is ambiguous, and it MUST be non-zero. Omitting the field means no indicator is given.

Five bits of the indicator are registered, so the acceptable values are currently 1 to 31. The bit positions are Reference Values (0), Endorsements (1), Evidence (2), Attestation Results (3) and Appraisal Policy (4). A value of 3 therefore means the content holds both Reference Values and Endorsements.
sections.eli5: A Record is a labeled parcel: one slot says what kind of thing is inside, one holds the thing, and an optional sticker says what job the thing does.

sections.title: The Tag CMW and Plugging in New Types
sections.content:
A Tag CMW is a CBOR tag whose number is derived from a CoAP Content-Format ID using the TN() transform from RFC 9277. These tag numbers fall in the range 1668546817 to 1668612095. The message is first serialized as its Content-Format says, wrapped in a CBOR byte string, and then prefixed with the tag.

Two CDDL macros describe the result: tag-cm-cbor for messages that are themselves CBOR, and tag-cm-data for all other types.

To add a new Tag CMW, the $cbor-tag type socket is extended with one more instance of a macro. For example, a CBOR message type with tag 1668612069 is added as $cbor-tag /= tag-cm-cbor<1668612069, my-evidence>. This is what lets a CMW stack accept new message types without changing its core.
sections.eli5: A Tag is a shortcut label printed straight on the box. To teach the system a new kind of box, you just add one more label to its list.

sections.title: Collections and Demuxing
sections.content:
Layered Attesters and composite devices produce Evidence in several parts. A server might have one attesting environment for its main CPU, another for a SmartNIC and a third for a GPU. A Collection CMW bundles such parts: it is a CBOR map or JSON object of CMW items, each under a label that is unique within the collection. Order does not matter. A collection MUST have at least one entry, and it can mix message types or cover several devices.

The reserved key __cmwc_t optionally gives the whole collection a type, either an absolute URI or an absolute OID. It works like an EAT profile at a higher level and defines the namespace in which labels are interpreted. Because collections can nest, implementations MAY limit nesting depth.

A receiver must also know which decoder to use. This is normally settled by the media type, the Content-Format, or the container (a JWT, CWT or X.509 extension). The RFC also gives informational pseudocode showing that looking at the first byte is enough to tell the forms apart, and says implementations are not expected to follow it.
sections.eli5: A Collection is a box that holds several smaller labeled boxes, such as one report from each part of a computer.

sections.title: Signing and Carrying CMWs
sections.content:
The CMW is only an encapsulation, so the RFC describes ways to add protection and to embed it in other formats.

  • COSE_Sign1: a CBOR CMW can be signed. The payload MUST be the CBOR-encoded Tag, Record or Collection CMW, and the protected header MUST contain the algorithm and either the media type application/cmw+cbor or the CoAP Content-Format 273.
  • JWS: a JSON CMW can be signed using the Flattened JSON or Compact Serialization. The protected header MUST contain the algorithm and application/cmw+json.
  • JWT and CWT: a cmw claim carries a CMW. A CWT claim MUST hold the CBOR forms (cbor-record or cbor-collection) and a JWT claim MUST hold the JSON forms.
  • X.509: a CMW extension may appear in certificates, CRLs and CSRs. It is identified by the object identifier id-pe-cmw (id-pe 35), holds either a UTF-8 string (JSON) or an octet string (CBOR), and SHOULD NOT be marked critical, though marking it critical is acceptable when legacy relying parties could otherwise bypass controls.

The RFC also notes that the TCG DICE format allows only a subset of this grammar, and in particular cannot encode collections.
sections.eli5: The envelope itself is not a lock. If you want a seal that shows nobody changed it, you stamp it with a signature or put it inside another trusted container.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
Record, Tag and Collection CMWs by themselves offer no authenticity, integrity protection or confidentiality. Each use case must decide which properties it needs. If the inner messages are already protected, the wrapper adds no new requirement; if they are not, protection must be added at another layer, for example by signing a record that holds an unprotected CWT claims set.

When a Collection CMW carries Evidence for a composite or layered device, all Evidence inside MUST be cryptographically bound together. Otherwise an attacker could swap Evidence from a compromised device for Evidence from a healthy one. The binding need not be one signature: it can use identifiers, linking claims such as nonces, or signing or hashing between members. The Attester that builds the collection is responsible for this.

On privacy, Evidence often contains personally identifiable information. Secure channels help, and a certificate authority that publishes Evidence claims in certificates should say so in its certification practice statement. Finally, any hosting protocol that embeds CMW must describe how it fits its own security model.
sections.eli5: An envelope does not keep secrets or stop tampering. Whoever sends it has to add a lock and seal, and make sure the pieces of a bundle cannot be swapped.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the following items for the CMW.

  • A cmw claim in the CWT registry with claim key 299, and a cmw claim in the JWT registry.
  • The +jws structured syntax suffix.
  • A new registry, RATS Conceptual Message Wrapper (CMW) Indicators, with the registration procedure IETF Review. Values 0 to 4 are assigned and 5 to 31 are unassigned.
  • Four media types: application/cmw+cbor, application/cmw+json, application/cmw+cose and application/cmw+jws. Each has an optional cmwc_t parameter that may be used only for collections.
  • CoAP Content-Formats 273 to 276 for these four types, which automatically allocate CBOR tags 1668547091 to 1668547094.
  • The OID 35 for the extension and 123 for its ASN.1 module.
sections.eli5: The official list of names and numbers was updated so that everyone uses the same label for each kind of envelope.
